questions.stem: Which sequence shows the organisation of a skeletal muscle from largest to smallest?
options: Muscle, muscle fibre, fascicle, myofilament, myofibril
Muscle, fascicle, muscle fibre, myofibril, myofilament
Muscle, myofibril, fascicle, myofilament, muscle fibre
Fascicle, muscle, myofilament, muscle fibre, myofibril
questions.explanation: A muscle is made of bundles called fascicles, each containing muscle fibres (cells); fibres are packed with myofibrils, which are made of actin and myosin myofilaments.

questions.stem: What are the two main protein filaments in a sarcomere?
options: Myosin and fibrin
Actin and myosin
Collagen and elastin
Keratin and actin
questions.explanation: Thin filaments are mainly actin and thick filaments are myosin; their overlap gives skeletal muscle its striped appearance. Collagen and elastin are fibres in connective tissue.

questions.stem: Even when standing still, some muscles are partly contracted. What is the purpose of this muscle tone?
options: Preventing blood from flowing into the muscles while resting
Maintaining posture by keeping the body upright against gravity
Producing heat only when the body's core temperature falls very low
Storing ATP in the muscle fibres for use in later exercise
questions.explanation: Continuous, low-level contraction of postural muscles such as those of the back and neck keeps the body upright. Muscles do produce heat, but that is not the purpose of tone.

questions.stem: According to the sliding filament theory, what happens when a muscle fibre contracts?
options: Actin and myosin filaments both shorten by folding up along their length
Myosin filaments lengthen and push the Z lines further apart
The muscle fibre shrinks because water leaves it by osmosis
Actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, so each sarcomere shortens
questions.explanation: The filaments themselves stay the same length; myosin heads pull the actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere, drawing the Z lines closer together.

questions.stem: What triggers the start of contraction inside a skeletal muscle fibre?
options: Oxygen binding to myosin heads when the blood supply increases
Sodium ions leaving the fibre through channels in its membrane
Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Glucose diffusing into the fibre from capillaries in the muscle
questions.explanation: A nerve impulse causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium ions, which bind to the regulatory proteins on actin and expose the myosin binding sites. Without calcium no cross-bridges form.

questions.stem: What is the role of ATP in the cross-bridge cycle?
options: It detaches the myosin head from actin and provides energy to re-cock the head
It forms the cross-bridge by binding actin directly to the Z line of the sarcomere
It is released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum to expose the binding sites on actin
It joins the actin filaments end to end so that the sarcomere becomes shorter
questions.explanation: ATP binding releases myosin from actin, and its hydrolysis re-cocks the myosin head ready for the next power stroke. Exposing the binding sites is the job of calcium, not ATP.

questions.stem: After death, muscles become stiff (rigor mortis) because ATP production stops. Which explanation fits the sliding filament theory?
options: Without ATP the myosin filaments break down and leave actin bound to the Z lines
Without ATP the myosin heads cannot detach from actin, so cross-bridges stay locked
Without ATP calcium cannot be released, so the filaments slide over each other freely
Without ATP the actin filaments shorten permanently and pull the Z lines together
questions.explanation: ATP is needed to break the bond between myosin and actin. When it runs out, cross-bridges cannot release and the muscle locks in place until the proteins later break down.

questions.stem: When a sarcomere contracts, which band stays the same length?
options: The H zone
The distance between Z lines
The A band
The I band
questions.explanation: The A band is the length of the myosin filaments, which do not change length. The I band and H zone shorten because the filaments overlap more.

questions.stem: Why must skeletal muscles work in antagonistic pairs?
options: A muscle can only pull when it contracts, so another muscle must pull the bone back
A muscle can only push when it contracts, so another muscle must push the bone back
Each muscle can only contract once, so a second muscle takes over afterwards
Two muscles are needed to produce enough force to move any one joint
questions.explanation: Muscles shorten and pull on bones through tendons but cannot push. Opposite movements therefore need a second muscle, the antagonist, on the other side of the joint.

questions.stem: During elbow flexion, the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes. Which terms describe their roles?
options: Biceps is the agonist (prime mover); triceps is the antagonist
Triceps is the agonist (prime mover); biceps is the antagonist
Biceps is the fixator; triceps is the synergist
Both are agonists because both are attached to the forearm
questions.explanation: The agonist is the muscle mainly responsible for the movement, here the biceps. The antagonist, the triceps, relaxes to allow it and later contracts to extend the arm.

questions.stem: When you lift a heavy box, muscles around the shoulder contract without moving the shoulder, holding it steady while the arm muscles work. What are these muscles called?
options: Stabilisers (fixators)
Agonists (prime movers)
Antagonists
Tendons
questions.explanation: Stabilising or fixator muscles hold a body part steady so that the prime movers can act efficiently. Tendons are connective tissue linking muscle to bone, not muscles.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the origin and the insertion of a muscle?
options: The origin connects bone to bone; the insertion connects muscle to skin
The origin is on the more fixed bone; the insertion is on the bone that moves
The origin attaches to the bone that moves; the insertion attaches to the fixed bone
The origin is the tendon at either end; the insertion is the belly of the muscle
questions.explanation: When a muscle contracts, its insertion is pulled towards its origin. For the biceps, the origin is on the scapula and the insertion on the radius.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares tendons and ligaments?
options: Tendons join bone to bone; ligaments join muscle to bone
Tendons and ligaments both join muscle to muscle
Tendons join cartilage to bone; ligaments join muscle to skin
Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone
questions.explanation: Tendons transmit the pull of a muscle to a bone, while ligaments hold bones together at joints. Both are dense connective tissue rich in collagen.

questions.stem: Which list gives functions of the skeleton?
options: Support, digestion, hormone storage, gas exchange and movement
Protection, excretion of urea, insulin production and movement
Support, oxygen transport, filtration of lymph and protection
Support, protection, movement, making blood cells, storing minerals
questions.explanation: Bones support the body, protect organs such as the brain and heart, act as levers for muscles, produce blood cells in red marrow and store calcium and phosphate. They do not digest food or exchange gases.

questions.stem: What gives bone both hardness and some flexibility?
options: Calcium phosphate salts for hardness and collagen fibres for flexibility
Collagen fibres for hardness and calcium phosphate salts for flexibility
Cartilage for hardness and red marrow for flexibility
Keratin for hardness and elastin fibres for flexibility
questions.explanation: Mineral salts, mainly calcium phosphate, make the matrix hard, while collagen fibres stop it being brittle. Bone with its minerals removed becomes rubbery; bone with collagen removed snaps easily.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the structure of compact bone?
options: It is made of osteons: rings of matrix around a central canal with blood vessels
It is a network of thin bony struts with the spaces between them filled with red marrow
It is made of chondrocytes in a firm gel with no blood vessels
It is a hollow tube of collagen with no living cells in its matrix
questions.explanation: Compact bone consists of osteons (Haversian systems): concentric lamellae around a central canal, with osteocytes in lacunae linked by canaliculi. A network of struts with marrow describes spongy bone.

questions.stem: Which cells are mainly responsible for building new bone matrix?
options: Erythrocytes
Osteoblasts
Osteoclasts
Chondrocytes
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts secrete new bone matrix and become osteocytes once surrounded by it. Osteoclasts break bone down, releasing calcium, so bone is constantly remodelled.

questions.stem: Where is spongy bone found, and what does its red marrow produce?
options: In the joints only; it produces synovial fluid
In the skull only; it produces cartilage
In the ends of long bones and in flat bones; it makes blood cells
In the shafts of long bones only; it produces new bone matrix
questions.explanation: Spongy bone fills the ends of long bones and the inside of flat bones such as the sternum and pelvis; its red marrow produces red cells, white cells and platelets.

questions.stem: Why does damaged cartilage heal much more slowly than broken bone?
options: Cartilage has no blood vessels, so nutrients reach its cells by slow diffusion
Cartilage cells cannot divide because they have no nucleus in the mature tissue
Cartilage is constantly broken down by osteoclasts faster than it can be made
Cartilage is made of dead cells, so it can be repaired only by surgery
questions.explanation: Cartilage is avascular: its chondrocytes depend on diffusion through the matrix, so repair is slow. Bone has a rich blood supply that brings cells and materials for healing.

questions.stem: Which type of cartilage covers the ends of bones at synovial joints?
options: Elastic cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Spongy bone
Hyaline (articular) cartilage
questions.explanation: Smooth hyaline cartilage covers bone ends to reduce friction and absorb shock. Fibrocartilage forms tough pads such as intervertebral discs, and elastic cartilage supports the outer ear.

questions.stem: The discs between vertebrae must resist strong compression. Which type of cartilage forms them?
options: Elastic cartilage
Articular cartilage
Fibrocartilage
Hyaline cartilage
questions.explanation: Fibrocartilage contains dense bundles of collagen fibres, giving it great strength under compression, which suits intervertebral discs and the menisci of the knee.

questions.stem: Which list gives the three structural classes of joints?
options: Hinge, pivot and ball and socket
Fixed, slightly movable and freely movable
Elastic, hyaline and fibrous
Fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial
questions.explanation: Structurally, joints are classed by what joins the bones: fibrous tissue, cartilage, or a fluid-filled synovial cavity. Fixed, slightly movable and freely movable is the functional classification.

questions.stem: The sutures between the bones of an adult skull allow no movement. How are they classified?
options: Synovial joints that are freely movable
Cartilaginous joints that are slightly movable
Synovial joints that are slightly movable
Fibrous joints that are immovable
questions.explanation: Skull sutures are fibrous joints in which bones are held tightly by connective tissue, permitting no movement. They protect the brain.

questions.stem: Which joint is a cartilaginous, slightly movable joint?
options: The joint between the bodies of two vertebrae
The hinge joint between femur and tibia
A suture between two bones of the skull
The joint between humerus and scapula
questions.explanation: Adjacent vertebral bodies are joined by intervertebral discs of fibrocartilage, permitting slight movement. The knee and shoulder are freely movable synovial joints.

questions.stem: Which feature is found in a synovial joint but not in a fibrous joint?
options: No movement between the bones
A fibrocartilage disc between the bones
A cavity filled with lubricating fluid
Bones joined by dense connective tissue
questions.explanation: Synovial joints have a capsule lined by a synovial membrane that secretes synovial fluid into the cavity, which lubricates and nourishes the articular cartilage.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a synovial joint type with an example?
options: Ball and socket: hip
Hinge: shoulder
Pivot: knee
Gliding: elbow and knee
questions.explanation: The rounded head of the femur sits in the cup-shaped acetabulum, allowing movement in all planes. The shoulder is also ball and socket, the knee and elbow are hinges, and gliding joints are found between the carpals.

questions.stem: A joint allows flexion and extension but not rotation or side-to-side movement. Which joint is it most likely to be?
options: The joint at the base of the thumb (saddle)
The elbow joint (hinge)
The hip joint (ball and socket)
The joint between atlas and axis (pivot)
questions.explanation: A hinge joint permits movement in one plane only, like a door, as at the elbow. The atlas and axis form a pivot joint, which allows rotation.

questions.stem: Why is the shoulder joint more often dislocated than the hip joint?
options: It is a hinge joint, so it cannot cope with movement in other directions
It has no synovial fluid, so the bones grind and slip apart easily
Its shallow socket gives a wide range of movement but less stability
Its deep socket restricts movement and strains the surrounding ligaments
questions.explanation: The shoulder's glenoid cavity is shallow, trading stability for mobility, so the humerus can be forced out. The hip's deep socket and strong ligaments make it much more stable.

questions.stem: What is osteoporosis?
options: A wearing away of articular cartilage that makes joints stiff and painful
An infection of bone tissue that causes fever and swelling
An overgrowth of bone that fuses the vertebrae together
A loss of bone density that makes bones fragile and likely to fracture
questions.explanation: In osteoporosis bone is broken down faster than it is rebuilt, so it becomes porous and fragile. Wearing away of articular cartilage describes osteoarthritis.

questions.stem: Why are women at greater risk of osteoporosis after menopause?
options: Falling oestrogen means bone is broken down faster than it is built
Rising oestrogen levels cause calcium to be removed from bone into the blood
Menopause stops the absorption of all minerals from the small intestine
Menopause causes cartilage to replace the bone tissue in the hip and spine
questions.explanation: Oestrogen helps limit bone breakdown, so when it falls at menopause osteoclast activity outpaces osteoblast activity and bone density drops.

questions.stem: Which lifestyle choices in youth help reduce the risk of osteoporosis later in life?
options: Smoking to suppress appetite and avoiding dairy foods
Avoiding sunlight completely and eating a high-salt diet
Weight-bearing exercise and enough calcium and vitamin D
Swimming as the only exercise and a low-calcium diet
questions.explanation: Weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone formation, and calcium and vitamin D are needed to mineralise bone, building a high peak bone mass. Smoking and inactivity increase the risk.

questions.stem: Which description best fits osteoarthritis?
options: Breakdown of articular cartilage, so bones rub, causing pain and stiffness
Loss of mineral from bone, so bones fracture easily after minor falls
An autoimmune attack on the synovial membrane that starts in childhood
A bacterial infection of the joint capsule that is cured with antibiotics
questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis is mainly a degenerative disease of ageing in which articular cartilage thins and breaks down; bones may rub and form spurs. Loss of bone mineral is osteoporosis.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with osteoarthritis of the knee is overweight. Which management plan is most consistent with current understanding of the disease?
options: Weight loss and low-impact exercise with a physiotherapist; joint replacement if severe
Complete rest of the knee for several months and a high-calcium diet to rebuild cartilage
Long-term antibiotics to clear the joint infection, followed by high-impact running
Vitamin D injections to harden the cartilage, with the knee kept in a cast
questions.explanation: Losing weight reduces load on the joint and strengthening exercise supports it; severe cases may need a knee replacement. Prolonged rest weakens muscles, and osteoarthritis is not an infection.

questions.stem: A bone density scan shows that a patient's bone mass is well below normal, though she has had no fractures. How does early diagnosis help her?
options: Her lost cartilage can be fully replaced by injections before the joint fails
The scan itself strengthens the bone by stimulating osteoblasts with X-rays
She can be given antibiotics to stop the infection spreading to other bones
Treatment and lifestyle changes can slow bone loss before a fracture occurs
questions.explanation: Detecting low bone density early allows medication, calcium and vitamin D, exercise and fall prevention to reduce the chance of fractures. Osteoporosis affects bone, not cartilage, and is not an infection.

questions.stem: In a hip replacement, what is replaced?
options: The damaged femoral head and the socket, with artificial parts
The muscles around the hip, with muscle taken from the thigh
The ligaments of the hip, with synthetic fibres only
The red bone marrow of the pelvis, with donor marrow
questions.explanation: A total hip replacement removes the damaged femoral head and lines the socket, replacing them with metal, ceramic or plastic parts. It is common for severe osteoarthritis.

questions.stem: Which bones protect the heart and lungs?
options: The pelvis and femur
The vertebrae and skull
The scapula and clavicle
The ribs and sternum
questions.explanation: The rib cage, made of the ribs, sternum and thoracic vertebrae, surrounds the heart and lungs while still allowing breathing movements. The skull protects the brain.

questions.stem: An older person spends six weeks in bed after an illness. Which change to the musculoskeletal system is expected?
options: Thicker articular cartilage because the joints are protected from movement
Stronger muscles because they have had time to rest and repair completely
Loss of muscle mass and bone density from lack of use and weight-bearing load
Increased bone density because the bones are no longer being worn down by use
questions.explanation: Bone and muscle respond to the loads placed on them; without weight-bearing activity, bone breakdown exceeds formation and muscles waste. This is why physical therapy and early movement are part of recovery.
